section.title: The Lord Our God Is Holy
section.sectionRationale: The last and most explicitly holiness-centered of the 'the LORD reigns' psalms, this hymn moves from the LORD's throne above the cherubim to His justice in Jacob and His answered prayers through Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, threefold repeating 'He is holy' as the ground of all true worship.
section.thesis: The LORD who reigns enthroned above the cherubim is a mighty King who loves justice and has always answered the prayers of His faithful intercessors, forgiving yet never excusing sin, so that His people are summoned three times over to worship at His footstool and His holy mountain because He is holy.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the reigning, holy King exalted over all peoples, verses 1-3; His love of justice and equity in Jacob, verses 4-5; and His pattern of answering His faithful intercessors, forgiving yet disciplining, verses 6-9.

units.label: The Lord reigns
units.note: the holy King exalted over all peoples

verses.text: The LORD {{malak|reigns}}; let the nations tremble! He is enthroned above the cherubim; let the earth quake!
Great is the LORD in Zion; He is exalted above all the peoples.
Let them praise Your great and awesome name, He is holy!

units.label: The mighty King loves justice
units.note: His justice and equity in Jacob

verses.text: The mighty King loves justice. You have established equity; You have exercised justice and righteousness in Jacob.
Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at His footstool; He is {{qadosh|holy}}!

units.label: He answers those who call
units.note: the pattern of Moses, Aaron, and Samuel

verses.text: Moses and Aaron were among His priests; Samuel was among those who called on His name. They called to the LORD and He answered.
He spoke to them from the pillar of cloud; they kept His decrees and the statutes He gave them.
O LORD our God, You answered them. You were a forgiving God to them, yet an avenger of their misdeeds.
Exalt the LORD our God and worship at His holy mountain, for the LORD our God is holy.

malak.gloss: To reign, be king. The declaration that the LORD reigns opens this psalm exactly as it opens Psalms 93, 96, and 97, forming a refrain that anticipates Christ's own eternal reign, Luke 1:33.

qadosh.gloss: Holy, set apart, wholly other. Repeated three times across this psalm, verses 3, 5, and 9, this word anchors the whole hymn; the seraphim's threefold 'holy, holy, holy' in Isaiah 6:3 uses the same root of the same God.

basic.context: This psalm closes the Psalter's 'the LORD reigns' sequence with its most sustained focus on holiness, repeating 'He is holy' three times. It moves from God's awesome enthronement above the cherubim, to His love of justice within Israel, to the pattern of Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, faithful intercessors whose prayers the LORD both answered and, where necessary, disciplined.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm's naming of Moses, Aaron, and Samuel is historically specific, real intercessors in Israel's real history, yet the psalm holds them up as a pattern for every generation of prayer, and its holiness refrain shapes how every act of worship, ancient or modern, ought to be approached.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm opens with the declaration that the LORD malak, reigns, the same word that opens Psalms 93, 96, and 97. Its recurring refrain names God as qadosh, holy, set apart, the very word the seraphim repeat three times in Isaiah's vision of God's throne.
basic.typology: The LORD enthroned above the cherubim, the mercy seat of the ark, anticipates the true mercy seat and meeting place between God and humanity in Christ; the pattern of forgiving yet disciplining intercessors anticipates Christ, the perfect and greater Intercessor whose prayers the Father always hears.
basic.christ: The LORD's reign proclaimed here finds its fulfillment in Christ, of whose kingdom Gabriel says 'there will be no end,' Luke 1:33; and where Moses, Aaron, and Samuel were forgiven yet still disciplined intercessors, Hebrews 7:25 presents Jesus as the perfect High Priest who always lives to intercede for His people and whose intercession never falls short.
basic.god: God reigns as an awesome, holy King who nonetheless loves justice and establishes equity among His people; He is near enough to answer the cries of His faithful intercessors, yet holy enough that even His forgiveness does not treat sin as though it were nothing.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 6:3 records the seraphim's threefold 'holy, holy, holy,' echoing this psalm's threefold refrain. Exodus 25:22 and Numbers 20:12 supply the background for the cherubim and for God's forgiving yet disciplining response to Moses. Hebrews 7:25 presents Christ as the perfect, ever-living Intercessor. Luke 1:33 promises that Christ's kingdom, unlike any earthly reign, will have no end.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's vision of the LORD reigning in holiness, loving justice, and answering the prayers of faithful intercessors while disciplining their misdeeds, runs forward to Christ, the eternal King and the perfect Intercessor whose prayers never fail and whose reign will never end.

context.literary:
Psalm 99 is a psalm with a refrain, and the refrain is its key. Three times the congregation is told that the LORD is holy: 'He is holy!' at the end of verse 3, 'He is holy!' at the end of verse 5, and 'for the LORD our God is holy' at the end of verse 9. The refrain grows as it goes, from a bare 'He is holy' to the full name and title in the last line. That gives three stanzas. Verses 1 to 3 look at God enthroned over the nations, verses 4 and 5 at the King's justice in Jacob, and verses 6 to 9 at how God dealt with Moses, Aaron and Samuel. Some readers divide after verse 5 and treat 6 to 9 as a single historical meditation, but the refrain shows the poet meant three movements.

Each stanza narrows. The first is cosmic: the nations tremble, the earth quakes, and the LORD sits above the cherubim. The second is national: justice and equity are established 'in Jacob.' The third is personal: individual names, a cloud, a call and an answer. The psalm brings the King down from the throne room of the universe to the conversation at the tent of meeting.

The summons also shifts. In verses 1 and 3 others are told to tremble and praise, in verse 5 'we' exalt, and in verse 9 the same 'Exalt the LORD our God' is repeated with a different place of worship, for the 'footstool' of verse 5 has become 'His holy mountain.' The way the verse echoes itself with a difference is typical of Hebrew parallelism, and it carries the reader from the footstool to the mountain.

The psalm belongs to a run of psalms that open with a declaration of God's kingship, Psalms 93, 96, 97 and 99, and it is usually read as the pair of Psalm 98 and the climax of that run. Psalm 98 closes on the King coming to judge in equity. Psalm 99 picks up the scene of His sitting in judgment and asks what kind of King this is, and its answer is a King who is holy, who loves justice, and who has both forgiven and judged His own people.
context.historical:
The setting is Zion and the temple. The phrase 'enthroned above the cherubim' describes the ark of the covenant, which had a golden cover with two winged figures, and Exodus 25:22 records God's promise to meet Moses 'above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim.' The ark was carried into battle at Shiloh, where the people brought the ark of the LORD of Hosts who 'sits enthroned between the cherubim,' 1 Samuel 4:4, and David brought it up to Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 6:2. The psalm's first hearers would have pictured that golden box as the place where the invisible King was thought of as seated. The 'footstool' of verse 5 is very likely the ark again, because David speaks of having it in his heart to build 'a resting place for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and a footstool for our God,' 1 Chronicles 28:2. Psalm 132:7 also says 'let us worship at His footstool,' at the place of His dwelling.

The three names in the middle of the psalm are the founders of Israel's worship and leadership. Moses is the lawgiver, who, though he was not a priest by descent, offered the sacrifices at the ordination and is called one of the LORD's priests here. Aaron is the first high priest. Samuel judged Israel and offered sacrifice and cried out for the people, as at Mizpah, where he offered a whole burnt offering and 'the LORD answered him,' 1 Samuel 7:9. These are the great intercessors in Israel's memory. The prophet Jeremiah names two of them together, 'Moses and Samuel,' as the pair whose prayer would normally have turned God's heart, Jeremiah 15:1.

The psalm's likely use is in pilgrim and festival worship, where the congregation moved toward the place of His footstool. The language of nations trembling suggests a time when Israel was surrounded by great powers and the claim that the LORD reigns could sound bold. The date is unknown, and nothing in the text fixes it. What is clear is that the psalm assumes the temple and the worship of Zion are in place, since verse 9 invites worship at 'His holy mountain.'

The psalm also assumes the long memory of Israel's failures. Verse 8 speaks of God as an avenger of their misdeeds, which only makes sense to a people who know the golden calf, the rebellion at Kadesh and the wilderness years, and who still see themselves as a people held by grace.
context.canonical:
Psalm 99 is strongly tied to the exodus and wilderness traditions of the Pentateuch. The pillar of cloud in verse 7 recalls the cloud that stood at the entrance of the tent as the LORD spoke to Moses, Exodus 33:9, and that covered the tabernacle from its raising, Numbers 9:15. The portrait of God in verse 8, forgiving yet holding to account, is a direct echo of the self-revelation at Sinai, where the LORD proclaims Himself 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished,' Exodus 34:7. Moses's intercession after the golden calf, Exodus 32:11, and the pardon at Kadesh, 'I have pardoned them as you requested,' Numbers 14:20, are the events the psalm has in mind.

The three-fold holy answers Isaiah's vision, where the seraphim call 'Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory,' Isaiah 6:3, in a scene where the LORD is 'seated on a throne, high and exalted,' Isaiah 6:1. The psalm is the song Isaiah's seraphim might have learned from. The same holy God is later the God whom Hezekiah addresses as 'enthroned above the cherubim,' Isaiah 37:16.

In the New Testament the three-fold holy is sung around the throne: 'Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come,' Revelation 4:8. The psalm's claim that God sits above the cherubim and is worshipped at His footstool is taken up by Isaiah 66:1 and by the New Testament's claim that the true dwelling of God is no longer a building. Stephen uses that Isaiah passage in Acts 7:48 to 49. The priesthood of Moses, Aaron and Samuel, the priests and the intercessors, is then fulfilled in the great High Priest who 'suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:12. Finally, the call to worship God 'with reverence and awe' because 'our God is a consuming fire,' Hebrews 12:28 to 29, is the New Testament's summary of what Psalm 99 means for the church.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wants his people to hold together two things that they are tempted to separate: that God is near and that God is terrifyingly other. The opening verses press otherness. The LORD is enthroned above the cherubim, the nations tremble and the earth quakes. A first hearer who was told this would feel small. Then the poet turns and says that this same King loves justice and has established equity in Jacob, and that He spoke to Moses and Aaron and Samuel from a cloud and answered them when they called. Holiness is not distance for its own sake. It is the quality of a God who is utterly unlike anything in His creation and who nonetheless draws near to a people and speaks.

The second aim is to give Israel a way of remembering its history as a story about God's character, not simply about its own heroes. The three leaders are mentioned, but each is praised for what they did: they called, and He answered, and they kept His decrees. The poet wants hearers to follow those patterns of humble obedience and prayer.

The third aim is to correct any presumption. Verse 8 is an uncomfortable line for a people who assume God's grace is a blank cheque. The God who forgave them was also an avenger of their misdeeds. The poet wants the hearer to come to worship with gratitude and with a sober awareness that the same holiness that forgives also holds to account. The refrain tells them what to do with all of this: exalt Him and worship, because He is holy.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes God's rule, His justice in Jacob and His past dealings with Moses, Aaron and Samuel, and it prescribes worship: praise His name, exalt Him, worship at His footstool and at His holy mountain. The descriptions are not set up as rules for believers to copy. The fact that God answered Moses, Aaron and Samuel when they called does not promise that He will answer every prayer the same way, and the psalm does not say it does. It says He is a God who answers and who forgives, and it invites the reader to call on Him.

The account of Israel's priests and intercessors is description, and it does not prescribe a human priesthood for the church. The New Testament is clear that the church has a single High Priest, Hebrews 4:14 to 16, and that the people of God are together 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9, so the psalm's leaders are models of intercession, not offices to revive.

Verse 7 says they kept His decrees. The psalm presents keeping God's commands as part of what marked these men, and so the prescription of the Law is part of the picture. But the psalm places obedience inside a relationship, since they called and He answered before they kept the statutes. Keeping the law is the response of people who have been spoken to.

As for the place of worship, the psalm's 'footstool' and 'holy mountain' describe the worship of Zion, and Christians are not asked to travel to a mountain. Jesus told the Samaritan woman that the hour was coming when worship would be in spirit and truth, John 4:21 to 24. What carries across is not the location but the posture, since the psalm calls for exalting and bowing before a holy God.

debates.question: Who or what is the 'footstool' of verse 5?

views.label: The ark of the covenant
views.case: The phrase 'enthroned above the cherubim' in verse 1 places the King on the ark, and King David speaks of the ark as 'a footstool for our God,' 1 Chronicles 28:2. On this reading the worshippers bow before the ark, the visible sign of the invisible throne.

views.label: Zion or the temple as a whole
views.case: Psalm 132:7 speaks of going to His dwelling and worshipping at His footstool, and Lamentations 2:1 says the LORD 'has abandoned His footstool in the day of His anger,' at a time when the temple and the city had fallen. Verse 9 of this psalm moves to 'His holy mountain,' and the footstool would then be the whole sacred place.

views.label: The earth itself
views.case: Isaiah 66:1 says 'Heaven is My throne, and earth is My footstool,' and verses 1 and 2 of this psalm set the cosmic scene of God over all peoples. Some take the footstool as a reminder that the whole earth is where He is worshipped.

debates.bearing: The views are not exclusive, because Israel itself held that the ark stood in the temple on Zion in a world that belonged to the LORD. Whichever is chosen, the footstool is a place where people bow low, and it does not shrink God to a place, as Isaiah 66:1 is quick to say.

debates.question: What is meant by God being 'an avenger of their misdeeds' in verse 8?

views.label: God judged the people's sins even as He forgave the leaders' prayers
views.case: The 'them' of verse 8 is the same as in verse 6 and 7, but the avenging can refer to the sins of the whole people that the leaders had prayed about. After the golden calf, God forgave at Moses's plea, yet He also said 'on the day I settle accounts, I will punish them for their sin,' Exodus 32:34.

views.label: God dealt with the leaders themselves
views.case: Moses and Aaron were barred from the land because they 'did not trust' the LORD at Meribah, Numbers 20:12. On this view the verse says that even His closest servants were forgiven and yet not exempt from consequence.

views.label: Both together
views.case: The verse says God is 'a forgiving God' and 'an avenger,' with no restriction, so it may sum up Israel's whole wilderness experience, in which both leaders and people were spared and corrected.

debates.bearing: Whichever reading, the verse refuses to choose between mercy and justice. Forgiveness in Scripture is not the same as the absence of consequence, and that is exactly the tension the cross later resolves, Romans 3:26.

study.originalLanguages:
Five words and constructions in this short psalm deserve a slower reading.

First, the refrain word qadosh, 'holy.' The root carries the sense of being set apart, cut off from the ordinary. The noun in Hebrew is often an adjective used as a name for God, and it does not describe moral purity alone but the whole otherness of God. The form is the same in all three refrains. In verse 3 and verse 5 the ending is 'He is holy' and in verse 9 the ending has the fuller 'the LORD our God is holy.' The BSB footnote at verse 3 notes that the Hebrew may also be read 'it is holy,' so the thing that is holy may be the name just mentioned, which would make the praise of 'Your great and awesome name' the subject of the refrain. Either way the point is the same, and the three-fold pattern is what Isaiah's seraphim echo.

Second, the verb in verse 1, 'let the nations tremble,' is from a root meaning to shake or be agitated, and the parallel verb in the next line, 'let the earth quake,' has the sense of swaying or staggering. The grammar of both is a jussive, a form that expresses a wish or a summons, so they are not simple reports. The first line of the psalm, 'The LORD reigns,' is a short Hebrew clause that can also be translated 'The LORD has become King,' and the same clause begins Psalms 93, 97 and 99 and is the heartbeat of the series.

Third, the name for the ark's throne, 'enthroned above the cherubim,' uses a participle of the verb to sit or dwell, yoshev. A participle describes continuing action, so the King is permanently seated there. The same phrasing is used in 1 Samuel 4:4, 2 Samuel 6:2, Psalm 80:1 and Isaiah 37:16, so a listener in Israel would hear it as a fixed title.

Fourth, verse 4 uses the phrase 'the mighty King loves justice.' The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew can also be read 'The might of the King loves justice,' so the power itself is given a love. The word for equity, meysharim, is the same one used of the judgment of the peoples in Psalms 96:10 and 98:9, from the root for straightness, and mishpat, 'justice,' and tsedaqah, 'righteousness,' close the verse. These are the three words that describe what a good king does, and they are what Psalm 72:1 asks God to give the king.

Fifth, verse 8 has two participles that hold the psalm's tension. 'Forgiving' is nose, from the root nasa, to lift or carry, the same root as Exodus 34:7, where God is 'forgiving iniquity,' which literally means bearing it. 'Avenger' is noqem, from a root that carries the idea of redress or requital, and the object is their alilot, their deeds. The two participles sit side by side with no conjunction between them in the Hebrew other than the 'yet' the BSB supplies, and they are both descriptions of a settled character. God is the kind of God who does both.

Finally, the verb 'exalt' in verses 5 and 9 is romemu, from the root rum, to be high, and in the same verse 2 the LORD is 'exalted,' ram, above all peoples. The people are told to raise Him higher in their speech than He already is in fact, and so praise is not a report of what is already obvious but an acknowledgement.

typology.type: The ark and the footstool, verses 1 and 5
typology.fulfillment: The ark, with the cherubim and the mercy seat, was the place where the holy God met His people and where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. John says 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, using the language of the tabernacle, so that Christ becomes the place where God's glory is met. Paul says God presented Christ as the 'atoning sacrifice,' Romans 3:25, the word used of the mercy seat in the Greek Old Testament. The type falls short because the ark was a box in a room that only one man entered once a year, while Christ is open to all who come, Hebrews 4:16.

typology.type: Moses, Aaron and Samuel, the called and answered intercessors, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: These three stood between a holy God and a sinful people and prayed, and the psalm says God answered them. Hebrews presents Jesus as the High Priest greater than Aaron and as the Prophet greater than Moses, Hebrews 3:3 and 7:25, and says He 'always lives to intercede.' Samuel's cry, which brought forgiveness at Mizpah, 1 Samuel 7:9, is a small picture of one whose intercession is permanent. The type falls short in that these men were themselves sinful and mortal, and Moses and Aaron were themselves shut out of the land, Numbers 20:12.

The cloud was the visible sign of God speaking to His servants and guiding His people, Exodus 33:9. At the transfiguration a bright cloud enveloped Peter, James and John and a voice said of Jesus, 'This is My beloved Son,' Matthew 17:5, and Luke's account adds that they entered it, Luke 9:34 to 35. The voice that spoke to Moses from the cloud now speaks about the Son and tells the disciples to listen to Him. The type falls short in that the cloud was a sign pointing to God's presence, while in Christ the speaker Himself becomes one of us.

The God who forgives and yet does not leave sin without consequence sets a puzzle that Paul says is answered at the cross: God presented Christ as a sacrifice 'in order to demonstrate His righteousness,' so as to be 'just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:25 to 26. Both halves of verse 8 are met in one event, in which the penalty is borne by the Son and the sinner is forgiven. The type falls short because in the psalm the consequences fall on the forgiven themselves, as they did on Moses, while in Christ they fall on Another.

typology.type: Worship at the holy mountain, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: Zion was the holy mountain where Israel gathered to worship. The letter to the Hebrews says believers have not come to a mountain that can be touched, but to 'Mount Zion, to the city of the living God,' Hebrews 12:18 to 22, and that we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, Hebrews 12:28. The earth trembling in verse 1 of the psalm becomes in Hebrews a shaking of all that can be shaken, and worship is now approached through Christ. The type falls short because Zion was a geographic place that could be lost, and the psalm knows it could be abandoned as Lamentations 2:1 says, while the heavenly Zion cannot be.

study.christ:
Psalm 99 leads to Christ through the themes that make it unique: holiness that draws near, priestly intercession, and a God who forgives without pretending sin does not matter.

Start with the throne. The psalm places God above the cherubim, above the mercy seat, and in Israel's worship the mercy seat was where blood was taken once a year for the sins of the people. Paul calls Christ the 'atoning sacrifice' in Romans 3:25, and the Greek word there is the same the Greek Old Testament uses for the mercy seat. The place where holiness and mercy meet has become a person. John opens by saying the Word 'made His dwelling among us' and that 'we have seen His glory,' John 1:14, which is the language of the tabernacle where the cloud and the ark were.

The psalm's three great intercessors fit together with the picture of the High Priest. Moses, Aaron and Samuel are named because they called on God and He answered. But the New Testament says that Jesus is a better priest in every way: 'Because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood. Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:24 to 25. Moses and Aaron died, and neither entered the land. Christ lives, and He brings His people into rest. Aaron's vestments, Moses's staff and Samuel's lamb were shadows. Hebrews also says Christ 'suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:12, which means that the holiness the psalm sings is a holiness given to His people by His own sacrifice.

The voice from the cloud deserves its own note. In verse 7 the LORD 'spoke to them from the pillar of cloud,' and the Gospels record a cloud again on the mountain, when the voice from it said, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him,' Matthew 17:5. In Moses's day the cloud spoke to the prophet. In the transfiguration it speaks about the Prophet, and Moses is standing there beside Him. The pattern is that the God who spoke from a cloud has now spoken through a Son, Hebrews 1:1 to 2.

Finally, verse 8 is one of the clearest pointers to the cross in the whole psalm. A God who forgives and avenges would be unintelligible if the forgiveness simply ignored the wrong. Paul says the cross is where both are true: God 'passed over the sins committed beforehand' and 'demonstrated His righteousness' at the same moment, Romans 3:25 to 26. The avenging of misdeeds fell on the Son, and the forgiveness was given to the people. The psalm leaves the two side by side, and the gospel explains how.

One caution. The psalm does not name Christ and does not give a prediction, and there is no need to make each detail, such as the cherubim, into a coded prophecy. The link is through the shape of the psalm's claims: holy and near, forgiving and just, a people helped by intercession. All three find their answer in the person the New Testament calls the great High Priest, who has passed through the heavens, Hebrews 4:14.
study.god:
Psalm 99 gives one of the most concentrated pictures of the holiness of God in the Bible, and what stands out is how much it holds together.

It holds together transcendence and nearness. The God who is 'exalted above all the peoples' is the same God who 'spoke to them from the pillar of cloud.' The two are not compromises between each other. The psalm presents the holiness itself as what makes Him worth approaching, because a God who was merely large would be frightening and a God who was merely close would be small. Holiness means He is like nothing else and yet He speaks to Moses, Aaron and Samuel and answers them by name.

It holds together power and justice. The psalm says 'the mighty King loves justice,' and the footnote says the might itself loves it. In the ancient world a mighty king was as likely to be a danger to justice as its guardian, and the psalm says that in the LORD there is no gap between the strength and the right. Justice is not a limit on His power but what His power is for. He 'established equity' and 'exercised justice and righteousness in Jacob,' verse 4, so His rule produces a people who are treated rightly, and that is part of why the nations are told to tremble and praise together.

It holds together forgiveness and accountability. Verse 8 is among the most balanced statements of God's character in the Psalter. The God who forgave is also an avenger of their misdeeds, and the Hebrew does not soften either half. It echoes the revelation in Exodus 34:6 to 7, where abundant love and forgiveness are set beside a refusal to leave guilt unpunished. A God who only forgave would not be holy, and a God who only punished would not be the God who answered the prayers of Moses. Both belong to the same settled character.

It holds together His rule over the whole world and His commitment to one people. He is 'great in Zion' and 'exalted above all the peoples.' Israel is not the limit of His reign but the place where His reign is most clearly known.

For worship, the psalm makes several demands. The refrain insists that the reason to worship is not what God gives but what God is: 'for the LORD our God is holy.' Worship begins with attention to His nature before it turns to His gifts. The repeated 'exalt' shows that worship is partly a matter of the body and the voice, bowing at the footstool. Moses, Aaron and Samuel show that worship and prayer belong together, since they 'called to the LORD and He answered.' And the trembling of the nations in verse 1 is a healthy fear that the psalm does not remove even for those who are near. Hebrews 12:28 to 29 says it this way: believers worship 'with reverence and awe,' because 'our God is a consuming fire.' The holiness of God in this psalm is not a problem to be managed but the ground of everything else in worship.

crossReferences.note: God promises Moses, 'I will meet with you there above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are over the ark of the Testimony.' This is the origin of the phrase 'enthroned above the cherubim' in Psalm 99:1. The ark was the place where the invisible King chose to be met, and the psalm uses its furniture to name His rule.

Isaiah sees the Lord high and exalted and hears the seraphim cry 'Holy, holy, holy.' The threefold holy of Psalm 99:3, 5 and 9 is the same proclamation. Isaiah's vision adds what the psalm implies: that the holy God's glory fills the whole earth and that seeing Him exposes uncleanness.

The LORD proclaims Himself compassionate and forgiving, yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. Psalm 99:8 compresses this self-revelation into a line and applies it to the wilderness generation, showing that the psalmist reads Israel's history through what God said of Himself at Sinai.

After the golden calf Moses sought the favour of the LORD and asked why His anger burned against His people. This is one of the times when Moses 'called to the LORD,' and the following chapters show both the forgiveness and the stated punishment that verse 8 summarises.

At Kadesh the LORD says, 'I have pardoned them as you requested.' The pardon follows Moses's prayer, which is the answered call of verse 6, but the next verses declare that the generation would not see the land, which is the avenging half of verse 8.

Samuel offers a burnt offering and cries out to the LORD for Israel, 'and the LORD answered him.' The same verb for answering is in Psalm 99:6 and 8, and this is the event that shows what Samuel's calling on His name looked like in a moment of national crisis.

The LORD says that even if Moses and Samuel stood before Him, His heart would not go out to this people. The verse shows how great their intercession was in Israel's memory, and how grave the later sin, so that Psalm 99 and Jeremiah read together show both the power and the limit of intercession.

When Moses entered the tent the pillar of cloud came down and the LORD spoke with him. This is the background of verse 7, where the cloud is the place of speech, and it shows that the psalm's God is one who communicates and not only one who rules.

The pilgrims say 'Let us go to His dwelling place; let us worship at His footstool,' and ask the LORD to arise to His resting place with the ark. It is the nearest parallel for the footstool of Psalm 99:5, and confirms that the word names the place of the ark and the temple.

The LORD says heaven is His throne and earth His footstool, and asks what house anyone could build for Him. This widens the footstool of Psalm 99:5 and holds the psalm in check, since worship at a footstool does not confine God to a building.

Since believers receive an unshakable kingdom, they are to worship with reverence and awe, for 'our God is a consuming fire.' The writer takes the psalm's shaking earth and holy God and says that the same awe is required under the new covenant, now grounded in gratitude.

The four living creatures never stop saying 'Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty.' The threefold holy of Psalm 99 is sung without end around the heavenly throne, and the church's worship on earth is a joining of a song already under way.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 99 answers a question the Bible raises at the very start: how can a holy God live with a people who are not holy? In Eden God walked with humanity. After the fall the people are driven out, cherubim are posted at the garden, Genesis 3:24, and the way to the presence is shut. Psalm 99 is set in a world where the cherubim have reappeared in a new way. They are carved on the cover of the ark, and the God they guard is seated among His people, at the centre of the camp and later on Zion. The psalm sings the marvel of that: a King who is holy, and who has nonetheless chosen to sit among a people He has to forgive.

It gathers up the story from Sinai onward. The exodus made Israel a people, the law at Sinai told them what holiness required, and the golden calf showed at once how easily they would fail. The shape of the relationship after that was mediation: Moses who went up, Aaron who offered, Samuel who cried out. The psalm tells that whole history in a few lines, and it says two things about it. God answered, and God did not pretend.

It sets up what is still to come. The priests and intercessors of the old order were all sinful and all died, and the people needed someone who could both represent them and be holy. The prophets speak of a King who will reign in righteousness, Isaiah 32:1, and of a day when the LORD will dwell among His people in a new way. The priesthood of Israel points beyond itself, and the letter to the Hebrews finds its answer in a single priest who lives forever.

The Gospels take up the language of dwelling, as the Word makes His home among us, John 1:14, and the cross, where holiness and mercy meet, takes up the language of the mercy seat, Romans 3:25. The church is then called a royal priesthood and a holy nation, 1 Peter 2:9, echoing Exodus 19:5 to 6, so that the whole people share in what Moses, Aaron and Samuel did, calling on His name.

The end of the story is the throne in Revelation. There the creatures never stop crying 'Holy, Holy, Holy,' Revelation 4:8, and the nations are to come and worship before the One who alone is holy, Revelation 15:4. The footstool and holy mountain become the city where God dwells with His people, and nothing unclean is admitted, Revelation 21:27. What the psalm could only see from a distance, worshippers gathered around the King, will be the whole creation's life. The cherubim are no longer posted at the gate, and the refrain that Israel sang three times is sung without end.

quiz.q: What word is repeated three times across this psalm as its central refrain?

options.text: "He is holy."
options.note: This refrain appears in verses 3, 5, and 9, anchoring the whole psalm's focus on God's holiness.

options.text: "He is merciful."
options.note: Mercy and forgiveness appear in verse 8, but the psalm's repeated threefold refrain is specifically 'He is holy,' not 'He is merciful.'

options.text: "He is silent."
options.note: The psalm emphasizes that God speaks and answers, the opposite of silence.

options.text: "He is distant."
options.note: The psalm actually emphasizes God's nearness in answering prayer, not distance.

quiz.q: Where is the LORD said to be enthroned in verse 1?

options.text: Above the cherubim.
options.note: Verse 1 pictures the LORD enthroned above the cherubim, recalling the mercy seat of the ark.

options.text: On a throne of pure gold in a human palace.
options.note: The specific image given is enthronement above the cherubim, not a human palace.

options.text: Beneath the earth in the depths.
options.note: The psalm pictures the LORD enthroned above the cherubim, not beneath the earth.

options.text: On Mount Sinai alone, with no further location named.
options.note: Sinai is not named here; the specific enthronement image is above the cherubim, later tied to Zion, His holy mountain.

quiz.q: Which three intercessors are named in verse 6 as those who called on the LORD and were answered?

options.text: Moses, Aaron, and Samuel.
options.note: Verse 6 names exactly these three as priests and intercessors whose prayers the LORD answered.

options.text: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
options.note: These patriarchs are foundational elsewhere in Scripture, but this psalm specifically names Moses, Aaron, and Samuel.

options.text: David, Solomon, and Elijah.
options.note: These figures are significant elsewhere, but verse 6 specifically names Moses, Aaron, and Samuel.

options.text: Noah, Job, and Daniel.
options.note: This trio appears together in Ezekiel 14:14, but this psalm specifically names Moses, Aaron, and Samuel.

quiz.q: How does verse 8 describe God's response to His intercessors' misdeeds?

options.text: He was a forgiving God to them, yet an avenger of their misdeeds.
options.note: Verse 8 holds together real forgiveness with real consequence for wrongdoing, as in God's dealings with Moses at the rock.

options.text: He forgave them completely with no consequence whatsoever.
options.note: The verse explicitly pairs forgiveness with being 'an avenger of their misdeeds,' so consequence is present.

options.text: He rejected their prayers outright because of their sin.
options.note: The psalm states God answered them and forgave them, not that He rejected their prayers.

options.text: He ignored their misdeeds entirely as irrelevant.
options.note: The verse specifically states God was an avenger of their misdeeds, so their sin was not treated as irrelevant.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament present Christ in relation to this psalm's picture of intercessors like Moses, Aaron, and Samuel?

options.text: As the perfect, ever-living Intercessor whose prayers for His people never fail, unlike those earlier intercessors.
options.note: Hebrews 7:25 presents Jesus as saving completely those who come to God through Him because He always lives to intercede.

options.text: As simply one more flawed intercessor no different from Moses or Aaron.
options.note: Hebrews presents Christ's intercession as perfect and unfailing, in contrast to the earlier, flawed human intercessors.

options.text: As someone who replaces the need for any intercession at all.
options.note: Hebrews presents Christ as actively interceding, not as eliminating the category of intercession.

options.text: As only a future intercessor, not yet active in the present.
options.note: Hebrews 7:25 describes Christ as one who 'always lives' to intercede, a present and ongoing reality, not merely a future one.

questions: This psalm's refrain, 'He is holy,' shapes everything else it says about God's reign, justice, and answered prayer. How does a fresh sense of God's holiness change the way you approach Him today?

Moses, Aaron, and Samuel are remembered as those who called on the LORD and were answered, yet they were also disciplined for their failures. Where do you need both the confidence to keep praying and the humility to accept God's correction?
The mighty King is said to love justice and to have established equity in Jacob. Where in your own relationships or community might you need to actively pursue justice rather than merely wish for it?

Verse 8 holds together real forgiveness and real consequence, God was forgiving, yet an avenger of misdeeds. How do you tend to distort this balance, either presuming on cheap grace or living in fear that forgiveness is not real?
Hebrews presents Christ as the perfect Intercessor whose prayers never fail. How does knowing that Jesus is right now interceding for you change how you bring your needs to God this week?

translationNotes.note: The cherubim above which the LORD is enthroned recall the two golden cherubim over the ark's mercy seat, Exodus 25:18-22, the place where God's presence met with Israel.
God's 'footstool' is elsewhere identified with the ark or the temple itself, 1 Chronicles 28:2, and in Isaiah 66:1 with the whole earth, showing the term's flexible but consistently reverent use.

The description of God as forgiving yet an avenger of misdeeds likely alludes to Numbers 20:1-13, where Moses himself, though forgiven, was barred from entering the promised land for striking the rock rather than speaking to it as commanded.
